# Summary

The author argues that the standard LLM security diagram—showing four attack types (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, context poisoning, output injection) with mitigations at each stage—misses the critical insight that real security must live in deterministic code the model never touches. Rather than building probabilistic classifiers at each stage of the pipeline, effective defense requires enumerating the finite set of actions your system is allowed to take (tools, database queries, destinations) and checking every model output against that enumerated boundary before execution. The four-box diagram correctly identifies real threats but trains teams to patch the wrong layer; the actual security surface is where model proposals cross into consequences, not where attacks enter the system.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the post's central argument about deterministic boundaries versus probabilistic classifiers, correctly identifies the four attack types mentioned, and faithfully represents the key insight about enumerating allowed actions rather than chasing attack patterns.
